cim_eredeti: Writing Artificial Intelligence Into Constitutions: A Global Constitutional Moment for the Algorithmic State
szoveg_eredeti:
–Boldizsár Szentgáli-Tóth, senior research fellow of the ELTE Centre for Social Sciences, Institute for Legal Studies (Budapest) and lawyer at the K-Monitor Public Benefit Association (Budapest), and Rebeka Kiss, junior research fellow of the ELTE Centre for Social Sciences, Institute for Legal Studies (Budapest)

Every technological rupture eventually reaches the constitutional lawyer’s desk. The printing press, nuclear energy and the internet each raised the question whether existing constitutional categories could absorb the new phenomenon. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the latest arrival, and from Santiago to Athens the temptation to reach for the constitution is strong. If an algorithmic system decides who is flagged for a tax audit, matches a face in a crowd to a name in a database and shapes how public administration reasons about individual cases, many conclude that the highest law should say something about it. For the most part it already does, through general rights guarantees. However, almost everything we want from the “constitutional governance of AI” is best placed in instruments that can be revised as understanding improves, and only a narrow residue belongs in the constitutional text itself. That is why a constitutional drafting moment is exactly when that residue should be identified with precision.

The issue is no longer hypothetical: states around the world now operate AI-based decision-support systems in welfare, policing, migration and taxation. This is a global constitutional moment, and constitutional drafters have begun to respond in registers as different as a binding Council of Europe treaty; national amendments in Chile and Brazil; proposals in Greece, Mexico and Minnesota; and a steady stream of court rulings in the Netherlands and France extending old guarantees to new machines. Occasionally a fresh drafting process makes the stakes unusually concrete, as in Hungary. The party that won a constitutional majority on 12 April 2026 has announced a broader participatory process for an entirely new constitution. A country whose 2011 Fundamental Law became an instrument of the majority that wrote it must now decide what a constitution can do about a technology of state power. That makes Hungary a clear test of our claim, because it pulls apart the two things the debate continues to conflate: incorporating a guarantee, and having an institution willing to enforce it.

The instinct to constitutionalize the state’s use of AI rests on a genuine intuition. Constitutional norms enjoy a durability and a symbolic weight that statutes cannot match: they bind the legislature itself, they structure judicial review, and they express foundational commitments in a form that a transient majority cannot easily undo, whereas a statute on automated decision-making binds only the majority willing to be bound. That is why several scholars speak of an emerging “algorithmic constitutionalism” as a next frontier of constitutional law. As Pollicino and De Gregorio observe, the diffusion of AI reshapes how public and private power is exercised, and the constitutional response should be to reframe the existing apparatus of fundamental rights rather than to abandon it. That reframing has to reach beyond the state to the corporations that build and control the underlying models, whose command of data, compute and infrastructure can rival public power.

Comparative practice already shows drafters acting on that instinct, though for AI so far only in proposals. Chile’s 2021 constitutional reform on neurorights protected brain activity and the data derived from it before the technology matured, not as a self-executing right but as a mandate to the legislature, and the Chilean Supreme Court later applied it against a technology company. The move signaled that some threats to the person are grave enough for the founding document rather than a data-protection code. The case for new rights, made most influentially by Marcello Ienca and Roberto Andorno, invites the obvious parallel: if neurotechnology warrants constitutional protection of the mind, why should algorithmic power not warrant a comparable anchor?

This is a familiar problem of constitutional design, not a new problem about technology. Rosalind Dixon and Tom Ginsburg call this deferral: vague language that leaves the work to courts, or express delegation to the legislature through a “by law” clause. Deferral suits high error costs, where information is thin and a decision taken now is likely to prove wrong, which describes AI exactly. Ginsburg also finds that specificity aids constitutional endurance, but his reason is that detail signals the drafters’ investment and helps constitutional subjects coordinate on the bargain, which a technical definition of a moving technology does not.

The first difficulty is that AI is not a stable object of regulation, a fast-moving bundle of techniques whose capabilities, risks and vocabulary – “machine learning”, “foundation model”, “agent” – shift on a timescale of months. Constitutions are deliberately hard to amend so that they remain stable across generations, and to write AI into one is to fix, in the most rigid available legal form, a concept almost certain to be obsolete before the ink is dry.

The second is that constitutional specificity tends to crowd out interpretive development. The strength of abstract guarantees such as human dignity, equal treatment and effective judicial protection is that courts can extend them to circumstances the drafters never imagined. The German Menschenwürde guarantee has been applied to automated police data analysis, a context its 1949 drafters never foresaw. A narrowly drafted AI clause risks displacing this generative abstraction with a brittle enumeration, inviting the expressio unius argument that whatever it does not mention falls outside constitutional protection.

The third is that entrenchment can produce a false sense of security. A clause requiring automated decisions to respect human dignity is easy to write and close to empty, because it restates a guarantee that already exists. The hard work is technical: when a human must remain in the loop, what counts as a meaningful explanation, how to allocate liability, how to audit a model. That work belongs in the EU AI Act and data-protection law such as Article 22 GDPR, and a constitutional slogan risks substituting for it.

The algorithmic state is not a constitutional vacuum. When public administration deploys an automated system to decide individual cases, the ordinary apparatus of the Rechtsstaat already applies: legality requires a statutory basis, the duty to give reasons requires that the affected person be told why, and effective judicial protection requires that a court be able to review, which constrains systems whose outputs cannot be explained.

Courts in several countries have shown how this works. In 2020 a court in The Hague, applying Article 8 ECHR, halted the Dutch state’s SyRI welfare-fraud risk-scoring system, because the legislation gave insufficient insight into how the model worked, and those affected were never told they had been assessed. France reached the same conclusion from its own text: when its Conseil constitutionnel examined the Parcoursup admissions algorithm in 2020, it upheld the confidentiality of the local algorithms but required each institution to publish the criteria it had used once the procedure was over, deriving that duty from the accountability of public officials in Article 15 of the 1789 Declaration. It did not invent an AI-specific right; it extended an eighteenth-century accountability clause to twenty-first-century administrative technology.

Together these cases trace a shared principle of reviewability: the algorithmic exercise of public power is no exception to accountability and to the right to a remedy. None of these guarantees mentions AI, and none needs to, because their abstraction is what allows them to b
cim: A mesterséges intelligencia alkotmányos szabályozásának korlátai
lead: Az AI alkotmányba foglalása helyett a meglévő jogi keretek és a rugalmas törvénykezés jelenthetik a hatékony megoldást.
osszefoglalo:
Szentgáli-Tóth Boldizsár és Kiss Rebeka, az ELTE Társadalomtudományi Kutatóközpont Jogtudományi Intézetének munkatársai [elemzésükben](https://www.iconnectblog.com/writing-artificial-intelligence-into-constitutions-a-global-constitutional-moment-for-the-algorithmic-state/) azt vizsgálják, hogy miként kellene a mesterséges intelligenciát alkotmányos szinten kezelni. A szerzők rámutatnak, hogy bár a közigazgatásban, az adóhatóságoknál és a rendészetben egyre terjednek az **algoritmikus döntéshozó rendszerek**, az AI túlságosan gyorsan változik ahhoz, hogy merev alkotmányos szövegekben rögzítsék.

Az elemzés szerint a túl **részletes alkotmányos szabályozás** kifejezetten hátrányos lehet, mivel elavulhat, vagy beszűkítheti a meglévő emberi jogi garanciák értelmezési tartományát. A holland és francia bírósági gyakorlat már megmutatta, hogy a hagyományos jogállami elvek, mint az **átláthatóság és a jogorvoslati jog**, a meglévő keretek között is hatékonyan alkalmazhatók az AI-alapú állami döntésekkel szemben.

A szerzők hangsúlyozzák, hogy a részletes technikai szabályozást, mint a modell-auditálást vagy az **emberi felügyelet kötelezettségét**, az alkotmányos szlogenek helyett az olyan konkrét jogszabályokban kell rögzíteni, mint az [EU AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689) vagy a GDPR.
miert_szamit: A vállalkozásoknak és fejlesztőknek érdemes a **konkrét iparági szabályozásokra és az EU AI Act előírásaira** figyelniük, mivel a jogi kiszámíthatóságot és a megfelelőséget ezek, nem pedig az **általános alkotmányos elvek** határozzák meg.

prioritas.indok: Magyar kutatók elemzése az MI alkotmányos szabályozásáról, ami szakmailag releváns.

tenyellenorzes.esemeny: Szentgáli-Tóth Boldizsár és Kiss Rebeka jogi elemzést publikált a mesterséges intelligencia alkotmányos szabályozásának kihívásairól és korlátairól.
hibak: Az ELTE kutatóintézetének pontos neve helytelenül szerepel (ELTE Társadalomtudományi Kutatóközpont Jogtudományi Intézet / ELTE Centre for Social Sciences, Institute for Legal Studies), nem pedig Állam- és Jogtudományi Kutatóközpont.
A bekezdésekben és a miért számít szekcióban hiányoztak a kötelező kiemelések (félkövér) és az elsődleges forrásra mutató link.
